The roster is therefore a *byproduct* of what got crawled. Two things follow, and both are wrong for this product:

**1. Anyone named in a document becomes a tracked public figure.** A committee protocol names witnesses, petitioners, private citizens giving testimony, clerks. Each of them would get a slug, a page, and a timeline — and eventually an inconsistency flag. That is precisely the exposure the market-landscape wiki's legal section is about, and Israeli defamation law is stricter than the US law that section surveys. It is a defect, not a policy choice.

**2. Coverage becomes unknowable.** Requirement `5.10` makes an unknown figure a 404 rather than an empty 200, for good reasons. But a figure who exists with a thin timeline is the same problem one step in: a reader cannot tell "this is their record" from "this is the part of their record we happen to have crawled". A roster we chose lets the page say which sources and which period it covers; a roster we stumbled into cannot.

## The shape of the fix

- A **committed roster** is an input to acquisition, not an output of it: who we track, why they qualify, and which sources cover them.
- An extracted statement whose speaker is not on the roster is **not dropped and not promoted** — it is stored unattributed (or against a `pending` figure) so the raw record stays complete and a person can decide. Unknown is its own state here too.
- `ensureFigure` stops being reachable from the acquisition path; adding a figure becomes a reviewed change.
- The roster carries an **inclusion rule** — the written test a person must meet to be tracked — and the methodology page publishes it. For elected officials the rule is trivial; for commentators it is the whole of the defensibility, and an arbitrary list is the thing to avoid.
- A figure page states its coverage: which sources, from when.

## Requirements this adds

Doc-first, so these are leaves before they are code — under §1 (identifiers and the corpus):

- a speaker not on the roster does not create a figure
- a statement by an unrecognised speaker is retained, unattributed, rather than dropped
- a figure page states the sources and period its record covers

  person, what put them on it. Refusing the entry is what stops the field being optional in

-- Passages by speakers we do not track. Not tracked is not the same as not recorded:
-- dropping them would make the raw record incomplete and would decide at crawl time
-- something a person should decide, and promoting them would create exactly the tracked
-- figure a roster exists to prevent (issue #31).
--
-- A table of their own rather than a nullable figure on utterances: these participate in
-- nothing analysis does — no cluster, no stance, no finding — and what they actually are
-- is a queue of decisions waiting for a person, which is easier to read as its own list.
CREATE TABLE unattributed (
  id           TEXT PRIMARY KEY,          -- ULID, minted once
  source_id    TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES sources(id),
  -- The speaker's name exactly as the document wrote it. Never normalized towards a
  -- roster name: the whole question about this row is whether those are the same person.
  speaker_name TEXT NOT NULL,
  speaker_role TEXT,
  -- Its position in the payload, so the statements that did resolve keep theirs and
  -- adding this speaker to the roster later moves nobody's id.
  ordinal      INTEGER NOT NULL,
  quote        TEXT NOT NULL,
  language     TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (language IN ('he', 'en')),
  said_at      TEXT,
  context      TEXT,
  created_at   TEXT NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE (source_id, ordinal)
);

CREATE INDEX unattributed_by_speaker ON unattributed (speaker_name);
SQL

git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'MSG' && git push -u origin claude/hitbut-roster 2>&1 | tail -3
Make the roster an input to acquisition, not an output of it

`runAcquisition` called `ensureFigure` for every speaker an extractor named,
and `ensureFigure` created the figure when the name was new. So the roster was
whatever got crawled: a committee protocol names witnesses, petitioners and
clerks, and each of them would have got a slug, a page, a timeline and
eventually an inconsistency flag.

Who we track is now a committed file. `syncRoster` is the only path that creates
a figure and acquisition cannot reach it; `ensureFigure` is gone. Ids are
carried by the entry rather than minted from the name, so renaming somebody in
the roster moves no citation — `roster-add` mints the slug once, when the entry
is drafted.

A speaker the roster does not name is neither dropped nor promoted: the passage
is held in `unattributed` under the name the document wrote, with its position
in the payload, so the statements that did resolve keep their ids and adding
that speaker later moves nobody.

Every entry must say what put its person on the roster. For an elected official
that is a formality; for a commentator it is the whole of the defensibility, and
the file is refused rather than the entry so a roster cannot half load.

Every person in the committed roster is invented, as everything else in this
repository is, until the defamation-law review in #28 has landed.

Refs #31, #28

input.title: A figure page must state what its record covers, and the methodology page must publish the inclusion rule
input.body:
The half of #31 that is a surface rather than a store. The backend half — the roster as a committed input, unrostered speakers held rather than promoted, `qualifies` required — is done; these two are not, and both are what make the roster legible to a reader rather than only to us.

**A figure page states its coverage.** #31's second argument: a figure who exists with a thin timeline is `5.10`'s problem one step in — a reader cannot tell "this is their record" from "this is the part of their record we happen to have crawled". Every roster entry now carries `coverage` (which source modules reach them, and from when), so the page can say it. Until it does, the data is there and nobody sees it.

**The methodology page publishes the inclusion rule.** Every entry carries `qualifies`, the written test that person meets. #31 is explicit that for commentators this *is* the defensibility — the difference between a roster and an arbitrary list of people someone decided to scrutinise is that the first can say, per person, what put them on it. A rule we hold privately is not that.

## What this needs

- A leaf under §1 or §6 for the coverage statement, and one for the published rule.
- Both are screen-kind: new goldens on the figure page and the methodology page.
- The API has to carry `coverage` and `qualifies` out to the site — neither is on the wire today.

Deliberately split out of the roster PR: that change is a defect fix in the store and the acquisition path, and these two are a surface change with goldens to review. Neither blocks the other.

Refs #31, #28

input.title: Make the roster an input to acquisition, not an output of it
input.head: claude/hitbut-roster
input.body:
Fixes the defect in #31. `runAcquisition` called `ensureFigure` for every speaker an extractor named, and `ensureFigure` created the figure when the name was new — so the roster was whatever got crawled. A committee protocol names witnesses, petitioners, private citizens giving testimony and clerks, and each of them would have got a slug, a page, a timeline and eventually an inconsistency flag. The case for `1.14` is that protocol, verbatim in shape: one tracked member and three people who should never have become tracked figures. ## What changed **The roster is a committed file, and `syncRoster` is the only path that creates a figure.** `ensureFigure` is gone — not renamed, gone — so acquisition cannot reach it and the compiler enumerated every other place that had been leaning on it. **Ids come from the entry, not from the name.** `ensureFigure` keyed on `display_name`, which meant a rename would have minted a second figure — exactly the failure `1.1` exists to prevent, sitting one roster edit away. `roster-add` mints the slug once, when the entry is drafted, and the entry carries it forever. `1.1`'s case now proves that by renaming through the roster and asserting the id holds and no second person appears. **An unrostered speaker is held, not dropped and not promoted.** `unattributed` keeps the passage under the name the document wrote — never normalized towards a roster name, since whether those are the same person is the entire open question — along with its position in the payload. That ordinal is what makes `1.15` matter: the statements that *did* resolve keep the positions they had, so adding that speaker to the roster later moves nobody's citation. **Every entry says what put its person on the roster.** `qualifies` is required and the file is refused rather than the entry, because a roster half loaded is a roster that has silently stopped tracking somebody. For an elected official it is a formality; for a commentator #31 is right that it is the whole of the defensibility. Every person in `data/roster.json` is invented, as everything else in this repository is, until the defamation-law review in #28 has landed. The file carries that warning itself — it is `{ note, entries }` rather than a bare array precisely so JSON has somewhere to put one. ## Seeing it fail Doc-first: `1.14`–`1.16` went into the spec first and the coverage gate went red for exactly those three. The change also produced an unplanned see-it-fail worth reporting. Mid-way, `3.5` (batch isolation) went red — its healthy document's speaker was not on the sample roster, so it was held instead of stored. That was the new behaviour working on a case that was not about it, and it is the reason the acquisition stand-in is a separate roster entry rather than a fourth person in `SAMPLE_ROSTER`: the seeded corpus is what the API and the screen goldens read, and an extra person there shows up in every listing and every picture. The server lane caught that leak too, on `5.1`. ## Folders touched
**`data/`** — new. `roster.json`: who the product tracks, why each person qualifies, and which sources reach them from when. Three invented people. **`src/backend/corpus/`** — `roster.ts` (the shape and its validator), `roster-data.ts` (the one place the file's location is spelled), `0004_unattributed.sql`. `store.ts` loses `ensureFigure` and gains `syncRoster`, `resolveSpeaker`, `recordUnattributed`, `unattributed`. **`src/backend/acquisition/`** — `run.ts` resolves each speaker against the roster and holds the ones it does not recognise; `ModuleOutcome` gains an `unattributed` count so a pass reports what it set aside. **`src/backend/`** — `index.ts` syncs the roster before each scheduled pass, so a reviewed change to who we track reaches the corpus on the next run. **`src/shared/`** — the `Unattributed` type: no figure id, no cluster, no stance, because it is a decision waiting for a person rather than a record about a figure. **`dev/tools/`** — `roster-add.ts` drafts an entry and mints its id against the ids the roster already holds. It prints; it does not write the file, because adding a person is a reviewed change.
## What this deliberately leaves #31 also asks that a figure page state its coverage and that the methodology page publish the inclusion rule. Both are surface changes with goldens to review, and both are now filed as #44 under #31 — the data they need (`coverage`, `qualifies`) lands here. #31 stays open until that half does. ## Verification `npm run typecheck`, `npm test` (58), `npm run test:server` (11, real workerd — which is also what proves the JSON roster import survives bundling into the Worker), `npm run test:screen` (9). `check_the_world.mjs`: 0 blocking. CI still cannot run — every workflow fails at startup, see #39. Refs #31, #28, #44 --- _Generated by [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code)_
